newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rouble redenomination heralds new era.
newsitem.headline: Rouble redenomination heralds new era.

text.p: Russia announced on Monday it will drop three zeros from the national currency, the rouble, at the start of next year, signalling confidence about the state of the economy.
Central bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin said the move meant the era of hyperinflation and economic stagnation was over and Russia was entering a period of economic growth and a strong rouble.
"We are sure we are putting a full stop not only to the period of inflationary illness, but to the economic decline," Dubinin told a news conference.
"All necessary conditions for transferring to economic growth in Russia are established."

In an effort to make the transition as smooth as possible, President Boris Yeltsin ordered that old and new money be in circulation for the whole of 1998. Old notes could be exchanged for new ones in the central bank until 2002.
Dubinin said that falling inflation and stable prices had encouraged the government to take the decision.
The consumer price index plunged to 14.5 percent year-on-year in June from over 1,000 percent in late-1993. The government forecasts inflation of just three percent in 2000.
Economists say the decline in gross domestic product, the broadest measure of goods and services produced in a country, has bottomed out.
"We hope the new heavy, firm rouble will firm in the future and its inflationary depreciation will slow down even more than this year," Dubinin said.
"We are sure we shall be able to support stability of the new currency rate against (fully) convertible currencies."
The foreign exchange market barely reacted to the redenomination news. There was an initial rush among dealers to snap up dollars, but rates soon returned to opening levels.
Dealers said the central bank was fully capable of holding the rouble rate within its pre-conditioned band due to its big hard currency reserves.
"We are fully ready to hold the rate in the current limits with hard currency interventions and reserves," Dubinin said.

From 1995 the central bank has been holding the rouble in a currency band, setting target rates for the start and the end of the year. As rouble's decline against the dollar is slower than inflation rate, it is in fact appreciating in real terms.
Dubinin said the central bank would not change its hard currency policy next year.
"I do not see any reason for a dramatic change in currency policy for 1998," he said. "The gradual devaluation of the rouble will most likely continue in line with inflation."
Last year Ukraine, Russia's neighbour and part of the former Soviet Union, chopped five zeroes off its national currency, karbovanets, and introduced a new unit, called hryvnya.
Ukraine's decision followed low inflation rates, steadiness of the national currency and considerable central bank reserves.
In Russia, the redenomination is a signal to the markets that the government has succeeded in its monetary policy, analysts said.
"The big news on Russia is that Russia is a significantly different risk than it was six months ago," said Mike Marrese, senior economist at Chase Investment Bank.
